newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean parties scramble to agree on labour law.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean parties scramble to agree on labour law.

text.p: A South Korean parliamentary committee agreed on Friday to water down key provisions of a controversial new labour law, but failed to agree on a blueprint for a replacement bill.
However, leaders of ruling and opposition parties were meeting to try to work out a last-minute compromise.

The law, which sparked almost one month of labour strikes after it was rammed through parliament last December, is due to take effect on March 1. But the government has said it will not be enforced in its present form.
President Kim Young-sam was forced to return the legislation to parliament in the face of bitter opposition from labour unions and criticism at home and abroad.
The committee of ruling and opposition parties agreed to delay implementation for two years of a controversial clause that would allow companies to lay off workers.
It also agreed to immediately recognise an outlawed union body that organised almost one month of strikes in protest at passage of the bill last December.
However, the panel was deadlocked on several thorny provisions.
These included articles making it illegal for companies to pay wages to workers for the time they are on strike and barring them from paying full-time union organisers from 2002.
"The committee is deadlocked over thorny issues," said Park Sun-suck, a spokeswoman for the main opposition National Congress for New Politics.
"Chief policy-makers of the parties are consulting each other over the next move," she added.
Park said the effort to forge consensus on the law may be turned over to parliamentary party leaders, or the task could be returned to the committee.

The issue of layoffs and free labour union association aroused the greatest passions among opponents of the law, which was rammed through parliament by the ruling New Korea Party with no debate on December 26 as opposition members slept.
In principle, the committee agreed to the introduction of flexible working hours -- a clause demanded by employers -- but was unable to fix the maximum length of the working day.

It weakened a provision that allowed companies to replace strikers with outside workers, agreeing only that replacements must be from within the company and allowing companies to sub-contract production.
The government said the new law was desperately needed to give companies the flexibility for global competition.
The outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions had called on Thursday for a half-day strike on Friday, but the response from workers was lukewarm.
Public transport and hospitals were not affected.

In an informal survey of about 20 companies under the confederation's umbrella, only two reported work disruptions -- Hyundai Motor Co and Daewoo Motors, which were at the forefront of strkes earlier this year.
Confederation president Kwon Young-kil has warned that the strikes could escalate into full-blown stoppages next week unless parliament bowed to worker demands.
"We are striking to show our unhappiness over the way the labour law is being handled in parliament," said a Hyundai Motor union official, who declined to be named.
